plot: Second person, daily-life format: you sign on with Black Sam Bellamy's pirate crew in 1717; eleven chapters answer why join, who is who, shares and pay, food, sleep, the articles, the chase, danger, the ship Whydah, the April 26 storm, and the last chapter is the mystery of the Whydah: found in 1984 under 5 feet of sand, the bell 'THE WHYDAH GALLY 1716' in 1985, and the treasure nobody has found.

beats.say: April 1717. A pirate ship called the Whydah sank off Cape Cod with about a hundred and forty men aboard. Only two of them swam to shore.
All hands! The wind is up, and a ship is running from us. Sign the articles, or get off my deck!
Wait! I only came aboard to find a job! What do I even sign?
This is a pirate crew in the year 1717. You are about to join it.
Why would anyone sign? How do you eat, sleep, get paid and fight? And what is the one thing a pirate ship did that no navy ship ever did?
And at the very end, a storm, a bell, and a treasure that nobody has ever found.
Chapter one. Why would anyone become a pirate?
You came from a navy ship, didn't you? I can tell by your back.
Yes. Bad food. Almost no pay. And the officers hit us with ropes for nothing.
That was real. A sailor in 1717 worked hard for little money, and the pay often came months late.
On a pirate ship, every man gets a vote. We even choose our own captain.
That's true. Pirates elected the captain, and the crew could vote him out again.
Chapter two. How do you end up on the ship?
Some men volunteered. Others were forced, especially if you were a carpenter, a doctor or a musician.
Pirates stole skills the same way they stole gold. A good carpenter kept a ship alive, so he did not get a choice.
And some were just kids. A boy named John King was about ten years old when Bellamy's crew captured the ship he was riding on.
Please! Let me join! I'll jump in the sea if you say no!
That's in the real record. He told his own mother he would hurt himself if they left him behind. She watched him go.
Chapter three. Who is who on a pirate ship?
The captain was Samuel Bellamy. He was only about twenty-eight years old, and people called him Black Sam.
But here's the surprise. In a chase or a fight, the captain gave the orders. The rest of the time, the quartermaster ran the ship.
I split the loot. I settle fights. If you break a rule, you answer to me.
The crew voted for the quartermaster too. Nobody got the job just because he was rich.
Chapter four. How do you get paid?
Not with a salary. With shares. After every ship they captured, the crew split what they stole by a fixed list.
Here's a real example from a pirate named Bartholomew Roberts, a few years later. The captain and the quartermaster got two shares each.
The gunner and the boatswain got one and a half. Everybody else got one share.
The gap between the boss and a regular sailor was just double. On a navy ship, the captain could earn many times more than you.
And if you lost an arm or a leg in a fight? Roberts's crew promised eight hundred pieces of eight. That's an insurance plan, three hundred years ago.
Quick question. What do you wear?
Whatever you stole. Silk coats, velvet hats and fancy buckled shoes were all taken from rich passengers and worn on deck.
The story goes that Bellamy wore his own long hair, tied back with a ribbon, when other rich men wore wigs. That may be where Black Sam got his name.
Chapter five. What do you eat?
Mostly hard biscuit and salted meat. After a few weeks at sea, the biscuit had bugs in it, and the meat was as tough as a boot.
Do I have to eat the bugs?
In the dark, you can't see them. Eat fast.
But pirates had a trick the navy didn't. When they captured a ship, they took the food too. Wine. Cheese. Sugar. Even fresh turtle meat.
The fresh water was another story. Kept in wooden barrels, it turned green and slimy within weeks.
Chapter six. Where do you sleep?
There were no bedrooms. You slept on the deck, or in a hammock, packed in close with a hundred other men.
It was hot, loud and smelly. On the Roberts ship, the lights had to go out at eight o'clock at night.
If you want to keep drinking after eight, you drink on the open deck. In the dark. No candle.
Chapter seven. What are the rules?
Every pirate signed a list of rules called the articles. They were serious, and they were written down.
No gambling with dice or cards. Keep your pistol and sword clean. And no fighting on the ship, ever.
So how did pirates settle a fight? On shore. Two men stood back to back, took steps, and turned to shoot. If both missed, they used swords.
And stealing from your own crew was the worst crime. The punishment was to be marooned, left alone on an empty beach.
Chapter eight. What do you do when you find a ship?
Raise the black flag! Show them the skull! Let them see who we are!
Here's something most movies get wrong. Pirates did not want to fight. A fight meant dead men and a damaged ship.
The flag was a message. It said, give up now, and nobody gets hurt. Fight us, and it will be worse.
Some pirates flew a red flag instead of a black one. A red flag meant no mercy at all, and ships that saw it were terrified.
Most merchant captains gave up without firing a single shot. And the pirates let them live, took the cargo, and sailed on.
So the scariest part is the flag. Not the cannon.
Chapter nine. What can go wrong?
Everything. Scurvy made your gums bleed. Fever killed men in a few days. And in a fight, flying splinters hurt more than the cannonballs.
There's a surgeon aboard. But his best tool is a saw.
Now for the boring part nobody puts in the movies. Cleaning the ship.
Barnacles and weeds grew on the bottom of the hull and slowed it down. So every few months, the crew pulled the ship onto a beach and scraped it by hand.
Two weeks of scraping in the heat. And nobody gets an extra share for it.
But even pirates liked to have fun. Many ships carried musicians, who played fiddles and horns to keep the crew's spirits up.
And the articles say the musicians rest on Sunday. Every other day, they play when we tell them.
When they reached a port with a lot of money in their pockets, many pirates spent it all in a few weeks on food, drink and parties.
A pirate's career was usually very short. Many of the famous ones were dead, hanged or gone within three years.
Chapter ten. The ship itself. The Whydah was built in London in 1715 as a slave ship, and this was her first trip.
Pirates captured her in early 1717, south of the Bahamas. She was fast and big, about a hundred and ten feet long.
The name Whydah comes from a port in West Africa, now called Ouidah. It was a place where enslaved people were loaded onto ships, and the ship was named for it.
They put in more cannons, raising the number from about eighteen to about twenty-eight. Now it was the flagship of a whole pirate fleet.
Historians think that roughly a third of the crew were Black men, some of them freed from slave ships, now voting equally with everyone else.
So in a few short months, a young man from the English countryside had gone from a sailor to the captain of one of the richest ships on the sea.
And the crew believed in him. They had a vote, they had a share, and they thought the ship would make them rich for life.
It was a rare thing in 1717. A ship where every man had a voice, and every man got a share.
By spring, Bellamy's crew had captured more than fifty ships. And now, the legend says, he wanted to go home.
There's a girl on Cape Cod. Maria Hallett. I'll go back rich and ask her again.
That's the legend. Nobody can prove the girl was real. But the ship really did sail north, loaded down with loot.
Whatever happens to this ship, remember it. We were free men, and every one of us had a vote.
That's the big idea behind the whole story. These were criminals. But their crews were run by votes, shares and written rules, long before most countries did the same.
So tell me, new man. Do you sign, or do you get off my deck?
Chapter eleven. The storm. April twenty-sixth, 1717.
That evening, a thick fog rolled in. Then a monster nor'easter hit, one of the worst storms ever recorded in New England.
Take down the sails! Get us away from the beach! Now!
The Whydah slammed into a sandbar. The masts snapped like twigs, and the ship rolled over.
The beach was only about five hundred feet away. That's one and a half football fields. But the water was so cold that a strong swimmer lasted only minutes.
Of one hundred and forty-six men aboard, only two made it ashore. Thomas Davis, the carpenter, and John Julian, the pilot.
The boy, John King, did not. In the end, the same ship he begged to join took him down.
Of the nine men who lived through that night, six were hanged in Boston later that year. The carpenter, Davis, was forced aboard, and the court let him go.
And John Julian, the pilot, was sold into slavery after he survived the wreck. The ship had been a slave ship. And in the end, a man from its crew was sold as one.
Chapter twelve. The mystery. Over the next few days, more than a hundred bodies washed up on the beach. And almost everything the ship carried was gone.
The governor sent a captain named Cyprian Southack to save what he could. He found the ship capsized, and the sand already swallowing it.
The wreck sank into the sand, and stayed there. For two hundred and sixty-seven years.
Then, in 1984, an explorer named Barry Clifford used Southack's old map to look for it.
It was lying in only fourteen feet of water, under five feet of sand. Searchers had been right on top of it, and had missed it for centuries.
But the pirates still had one proof to give. In 1985, divers pulled up a bronze bell, scraped off the crust, and read the words.
It said, The Whydah Gally, 1716. It was the first pirate ship ever positively identified.
Since then, divers have brought up more than two hundred thousand pieces. Coins, cannons, pistols, buttons, even gold.
They even found a tiny shoe, a silk stocking and a small leg bone. Scientists said it came from a child between eight and eleven. Most likely, John King.
But the real mystery is still down there. Old stories say the ship carried thirty thousand pounds of silver and ten thousand pounds of gold.
Even Clifford says it himself. They've never found what he calls the mother lode.
The treasure of the Whydah might still be buried somewhere under the sand of Cape Cod. Maybe right under the beach where families walk today.
So think about it. A crew that voted for its leaders, shared the loot, and paid for every lost arm. Would you have signed the articles?
Tell me in the comments, and subscribe for more true history.

long.title: Your Life at Every Rank of a Pirate Crew (1717) 🏴‍☠️
long.description:
Would you have signed the pirate articles? Tell me in the comments.

How did pirates really live in 1717? What did they eat, how did they get paid, who gave the orders, and what happened when the rules were broken? Follow the crew of the pirate ship Whydah, and then the storm that sank it off Cape Cod with only two survivors. At the end: a bell, a boy's shoe, and a treasure that has never been found.
